flashcards.q: What does 'cron is a lie about data readiness' mean precisely?
flashcards.a: A cron job runs at its fixed time regardless of whether upstream data actually landed. It has no mechanism to verify that assumption, so the one day upstream is late, the job runs anyway on incomplete data with zero errors thrown.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't padding a cron schedule (e.g. moving 2am to 4am) actually fix the readiness problem?
flashcards.a: It doesn't fix the structural issue, it just moves the threshold at which the same failure recurs (what happens when upstream is even later), while costing latency every single night to hedge against a rare event.

flashcards.q: What is the failure mode of an event-driven trigger, and why is it dangerous?
flashcards.a: It can silently stop firing (IAM drift, notification config removed, event pattern no longer matches) — producing nothing, no error, no timeout. It's dangerous because absence is much harder to notice than a loud failure.

flashcards.q: What's the necessary backstop for any event-driven trigger design, and why?
flashcards.a: An independent freshness/liveness check on the downstream table or system, decoupled from the trigger's own health signals — because the trigger's failure mode is silence, monitoring the outcome is the only reliable way to catch it.

flashcards.q: What capabilities does EventBridge for S3 add over native S3 Event Notifications?
flashcards.a: Filtering on arbitrary event fields (not just prefix/suffix), fan-out to many independent targets from one event, and archive-and-replay for reprocessing historical events.

flashcards.q: Standard vs Express Step Functions: execution guarantee, history, and typical use case?
flashcards.a: Standard: exactly-once execution, full history up to a year, long-running (up to a year) — audit/compliance workflows. Express: at-least-once, short-lived (minutes), no full history beyond CloudWatch Logs — high-volume, non-audit-critical work.

flashcards.q: Why does picking Express Step Functions implicitly require idempotent workflow steps?
flashcards.a: Express is at-least-once, meaning a step can be invoked more than once for the same logical event, unlike Standard's exactly-once execution guarantee which absorbs that concern for you.

flashcards.q: What's the standard AWS-recommended composition of EventBridge and Step Functions?
flashcards.a: EventBridge decides when/what triggers (the event/schedule layer); Step Functions handles what happens next — the sequencing, retries, and state of the actual multi-step workflow. Kept deliberately separate.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between EventBridge Rules and EventBridge Scheduler?
flashcards.a: Rules match events against a pattern (or basic cron/rate expression) and route to a target. Scheduler is purpose-built for scheduling at scale: millions of one-time/recurring schedules, native retries, DLQs, and timezone handling built in.

flashcards.q: How does SQS provide backpressure, and what happens if visibility timeout is set too short vs too long?
flashcards.a: SQS decouples producer emission rate from consumer processing rate; messages queue rather than overwhelming a slow consumer. Too short a visibility timeout: a second consumer grabs the message before the first finishes, causing duplicate processing. Too long: a crashed consumer's messages sit invisible and unprocessed for the full timeout.

flashcards.q: Why must every consumer triggered by SQS, EventBridge, or S3 event notifications be idempotent?
flashcards.a: All three mechanisms are at-least-once delivery. A retry or redelivery can invoke the consumer twice for the same logical event, and even Step Functions Standard's exactly-once execution guarantee only covers the state machine execution itself, not exactly-once delivery of the triggering event into it.

flashcards.q: What are the four diagnostic steps for a trigger that has silently stopped firing?
flashcards.a: 1) Confirm the producer actually emitted the event (source logs). 2) Check the event bus/notification config for drift (IAM, pattern match). 3) Check consumer invocation metrics for the exact time invocations dropped. 4) Check account-level quota/throttling.

flashcards.q: When is it still legitimate to use plain cron, knowing its readiness limitation?
flashcards.a: When the upstream's completion time has a genuinely tight, well-understood, rarely-violated bound with its own active, monitored SLA — managing the risk at the source rather than assuming it silently.
